tip: English says 'I am thirty' – Hindi states age as something you have: मेरी उम्र तीस साल है (meri umra tees saal hai = my age is thirty years).
Hindi has no verb 'have'. Family is stated as simply yours: मेरे दो बेटे और एक बेटी है (mere do bete aur ek beti hai = my two sons and one daughter are).
Owned things take पास: मेरे पास सिर्फ़ पचास रुपये हैं (mere paas sirf pachaas rupaye hain = by me are only fifty rupees). Family skips पास – bare मेरे (mere) for relatives.
Hindi counts big money in लाख (laakh = 100,000): दो लाख रुपये (do laakh rupaye) = 200,000 rupees. After thousand, the everyday unit is lakh, not 'hundred thousand'.
साढ़े (saadhe) before an hour adds a half: साढ़े तीन (saadhe teen) = 3:30. Only 1:30 and 2:30 use special words instead: डेढ़ (dedh) and ढाई (dhaai).
सवा (sava) before an hour adds a quarter: सवा चार बजे (sava chaar baje) = 4:15. A single word for 'quarter past'.
पौने (paune) subtracts a quarter from the hour named: पौने दो बजे (paune do baje) = 1:45, not 2:45. Hindi points at the hour that's coming.
No word for 'at' with times: नौ बजे खुलती है (nau baje khulti hai = opens at nine). The bare time expression carries 'at' by itself.
O'clock is plural: नौ बजे हैं (nau baje hain = nine have struck), with हैं not है. Only one o'clock is singular – एक बजा है (ek baja hai).
Minutes past the hour use बजकर (bajkar = having struck): बारह बजकर चालीस मिनट (baarah bajkar chaalees minute) = 12:40.
Dates commonly use plain numbers: तारीख़ बीस मार्च है (taareekh bees march hai = the date is twenty March). Hindi says 'twenty March' – no 'of' before the month.
Ordinals agree in gender: तारीख़ (taareekh = date) is feminine, so 'twenty-fifth' is पच्चीसवीं (pachchisvin) with -वीं, not पच्चीसवाँ.
दिन (din = day) looks the same in singular and plural: तीन सौ पैंसठ दिन (teen sau painsath din = 365 days). Masculine nouns ending in a consonant do not change in the direct plural.
होता है (hota hai) marks a general truth: बारह महीने का एक साल होता है (baarah maheene ka ek saal hota hai). Plain है (hai) = right now; होता है = always the case.
वाली (vali) turns a noun into 'the one with': बारह डिब्बों वाली (baarah dibbon vali) = the twelve-coach one. Hindi builds adjectives from nouns this way.
'Three times a day' is said with में (mein = in): दिन में तीन बार (din mein teen baar). बार (baar) is the word for 'times'.
Measures attach directly, no 'of': दो सौ ग्राम चीनी (do sau gram cheeni = two hundred grams sugar). Nothing sits between the amount and the noun.
Devanagari has its own digits: १९५० (1950). Indian signs, dates and prices switch between १२३ and 123 freely, so both sets are worth knowing.
Hindi keeps 'hundred' audible in years: उन्नीस सौ सैंतालीस (unnees sau saintalees = nineteen hundred forty-seven). English drops it – 'nineteen forty-seven'.
कम से कम (kam se kam = less than less) means 'at least': कम से कम बीस फ़ीट (kam se kam bees feet) = at least twenty feet. The doubling sets a floor.
The tiny word ही (hi) means 'as early as / right from': पाँच बजे से ही (paanch baje se hi = from five itself). Without ही it's just neutral 'from five'.
Time acts on you: हमें एक घंटा लग गया (hamein ek ghanta lag gaya = to us one hour attached). The hour is the subject; you are the target of the delay.
Where English says the book 'is' on the table, Hindi says its state: रखी है (rakhi hai = is placed/kept). Things sit, lie or are kept – not just 'are'.
पास here is the English loan 'pass': पास हुए (paas hue = became pass) means passed. It sounds like के पास (ke paas = near/have) – context separates them.
तक (tak) covers both 'by' and 'until': आठ बजे तक (aath baje tak) = by eight here. With deadlines it's 'by'; with ongoing actions it's 'until'.
Respect makes one person grammatically plural: पिताजी (pitaji = father) takes plural हैं (hain = are), not है. Elders and respected people always get plural agreement.
With ने (ne), the past verb matches the thing acted on: लिखे (likhe) is plural to agree with पाँच पत्र (paanch patra = five letters), not with 'I'.
Prices take में (mein = in): बारह हज़ार रुपये में ख़रीदा (baarah hazaar rupaye mein khareeda = bought in 12,000 rupees). Hindi says 'in' where English says 'for'.
